guides.title: Can a manufactured home go on my Horry County lot?
guides.description: Start with the parcel and the responsible office before choosing a home.

sections.title: Identify the property
sections.body: Bring the parcel identifier, an address if assigned, a sketch or survey you already have, and the proposed home dimensions. Ask which planning and permitting office has jurisdiction; a mailing town alone does not answer that question.

sections.title: Ask for the current checklist
sections.body: The county packet identifies address verification, a site plan, and sewer or septic documentation among its setup materials. Use it to prepare questions, then ask the responsible office to confirm the current requirements for this parcel.

sections.title: Keep a written decision log
sections.body: Record who answered, when, which parcel they reviewed, and which documents remain outstanding. Ask separately about allowed home type, setbacks, access, flood information, utilities, and any private restrictions. A nearby completed home is useful context, but does not establish approval for your lot.

guides.title: Land-readiness checklist for a home and lot
guides.description: Organize the unknowns before requesting an itemized project scope.

sections.title: Property and access
sections.body: Start a property folder with the parcel identifier, assigned address if known, ownership information, and any survey or plat you already have. Add the model dimensions and a sketch of where you would like the home to sit. Tell the team whether you own the lot or are still considering it. A listing address and acreage alone are not a site review. Ask which office has jurisdiction before relying on another property's approval.

sections.title: Check the delivery questions
sections.body: Describe the road, driveway entrance, gates, and visible obstacles along the proposed route. Photos can help explain a question, but the transport and installation team must determine whether access works for the selected home. Ask who will check clearances and turning space, what work might be needed, and whether that work is included in the estimate. Do not clear, grade, or purchase land on the strength of this checklist alone.

sections.title: Space and services
sections.body: Keep water supply, wastewater, and electricity as three separate questions. Note the provider or system if known, and gather existing connection or septic records. Georgetown's application distinguishes public water from a well and public sewer from septic; Horry's packet also calls for wastewater documentation. Ask the responsible office or provider what review applies to your proposed home. Existing service on a lot does not settle connection scope, capacity, or cost.

sections.title: Record what still needs an answer
sections.body: Ask about the proposed home location, setbacks, flood information, drainage, foundation, and any private property restrictions. For each question, write the responsible person or office, the document or visit needed, and the next follow-up. Use three simple statuses: confirmed in writing, pending review, or not yet priced. A nearby Home Placer project can help you discuss the possibilities, but it is not permission to place that home on your parcel.

sections.title: Scope and records
sections.body: Bring your folder and open questions when requesting a written home-and-land scope. Ask which items are included, which have allowances, which are excluded, and who handles each unresolved item. If you do not have land yet, say so; you can start a conversation without pretending the parcel details are known. This checklist organizes that conversation and does not certify a lot as buildable or establish a final package price.

guides.title: Conway, Loris, Longs and Aynor: verify the parcel first
guides.description: Use town-level project experience while checking the correct jurisdiction.

sections.title: Start with the exact parcel
sections.body: A search for a home in Conway, Loris, Longs, or Aynor begins with the same question: which authority reviews this specific property? Give the parcel identifier to the county and ask whether a municipal office also needs to be involved.

sections.title: Compare questions, not assumed approvals
sections.body: Ask whether the address, proposed home location, utility arrangement, access, and flood information are sufficient for the current review. Do not copy a permit checklist or approval from a different property without checking applicability.

sections.title: Use completed projects responsibly
sections.body: Home Placer’s existing archive contains sold projects in these towns. Compare the recorded model and lot context to frame a conversation. Historical projects do not establish present inventory, current price, or permission to place the same home on another parcel.

guides.title: Septic, sewer and water: questions before pricing
guides.description: Identify the service arrangement and the evidence needed for your lot.

sections.title: Separate water from wastewater
sections.body: Georgetown’s application asks separately about public water or a well, and public sewer or septic. Make the same distinction in your notes. Ask the relevant office or provider who confirms service, capacity, connection location, and the documents needed.

sections.title: Existing does not mean confirmed
sections.body: If a lot already has a well, septic system, or connection, gather existing records and ask what current review is needed for the proposed home. Do not assume a visible pipe or a seller’s description establishes suitability.

sections.title: Ask what the estimate covers
sections.body: Request separate written treatment of connections, taps, trenching, repairs, testing, and work still awaiting review. Ask who is responsible for each unresolved item and how changes will be documented before work proceeds.

guides.title: From land review to move-in: plan the dependencies
guides.description: A planning sequence with questions for the team, without a promised completion date.

sections.title: Before committing to a schedule
sections.body: First distinguish an existing listed home from a home that still needs to be selected, ordered, and installed. Ask the team which milestones are already complete and which depend on the parcel, home availability, written scope, or your lender. Do not treat a model photo as a ready-to-move-in listing. Keep one project record showing each open question, its owner, and what must be resolved before the next step.

sections.title: Confirm the parcel and written scope
sections.body: Gather the parcel information, proposed home dimensions, and records already available. Ask which authority reviews the property and which documents are missing. Horry's packet identifies a site plan and wastewater documentation; Georgetown's application records water and sewer arrangements. Ask the responsible office for the current parcel-specific checklist rather than assuming the same process applies everywhere. Put included work, allowances, exclusions, and responsibilities in writing before comparing schedules.

sections.title: Before delivery
sections.body: Ask who confirms permits, delivery access, foundation and site readiness, utility coordination, and the home's availability. Have the team distinguish an estimated delivery date from an actual delivery and from the installation schedule. A date on a calendar does not establish that preceding work is finished. Request the next milestone, its prerequisites, and a contact for changes; avoid booking a move solely around an early estimate.

sections.title: Track installation and remaining work separately
sections.body: After delivery, ask what installation, connection, inspection, and finish work remains in the agreed scope. Keep scheduled, completed, and awaiting approval as separate statuses. Ask who updates you when a dependency changes and when the schedule will be revisited. Factory construction is only part of a land-home project; work at the property and required approvals still affect the path to handoff. No fixed number of weeks is promised by this sequence.

sections.title: Before move-in
sections.body: Confirm with the team and responsible authority which final approvals and utility steps apply and whether they are complete. Request the handoff documents, warranty information, and service contacts for your actual home, and keep an agreed record of any outstanding work. Confirm your move-in arrangements against the home's actual status, not the model's marketing page. Planning milestones do not expand warranty coverage, and this guide does not establish a completion or occupancy date.

guides.title: Home, land and setup: compare the written scope
guides.description: Build a useful comparison before a financing conversation.

sections.title: Separate the decisions
sections.body: A model page describes a design you can discuss with Home Placer. An active land-home listing describes a particular home and property with its own price and status. A sold project is historical context, not a current offer. Start by identifying which of these you are comparing, then note the model, parcel, included work, and estimate or listing date. Two prominent dollar amounts may describe very different scopes.

sections.title: Understand the model estimate
sections.body: Home Placer's model package estimates include full setup and assume a quarter-acre lot. The model home-only estimate is $60,000 below that package estimate. That difference is an estimating convention, not a separate quote for a particular parcel or every utility connection. Lot size, land cost, site conditions, utilities, permits, and selected options can change the written estimate. Tell the team if you already own land so the proposed scope reflects your situation.

sections.title: Make unknown costs visible
sections.body: Request separate written treatment of the home, land, transport, foundation, site preparation, utility work, permits, and finish options. For each item, ask whether it is included, subject to an allowance, excluded, or still awaiting an estimate. Identify who pays and who performs the work. An allowance is not a promise that the final cost cannot change; ask how a change will be priced and agreed before work proceeds.

sections.title: Compare the same property questions
sections.body: Use the same parcel information when reviewing competing scopes. Ask who verifies access, home placement, water, sewer or septic, and power, and what written information is still needed. Horry's permit packet and Georgetown's application help identify questions, but the responsible office confirms the current requirements for the actual lot. Do not assume land described as available, or a lot with an existing connection, has already been approved for your selected home.

sections.title: Bring the same scope to the lender
sections.body: Give your chosen lender the proposed property and written project scope, not just a model's starting estimate. Ask which costs and documents their actual product addresses and request their written disclosures. Keep lender costs separate from the dealer's project scope so neither is mistaken for the other. Call, text, email, or send Home Placer your questions for a tailored written estimate. This checklist establishes no loan program eligibility, rate, payment, or approval.
